related_questions.question: What does a pre-stroke headache feel like?

text_blocks.snippet: A pre-stroke headache, also known as a sentinel headache, can feel like a sudden, severe headache that is different from your usual headaches. It may be a warning sign for a hemorrhagic stroke (bleeding in the brain) or an ischemic stroke (caused by a blockage). The headache may be mild to moderate, but can also be a "thunderclap headache," extremely severe and sudden. It can be accompanied by other neurological symptoms like facial drooping, arm weakness, or speech difficulties.
snippet_highlighted_words: a sudden, severe headache that is different from your usual headaches

list.title: Sudden onset:
list.snippet: The headache appears abruptly, not gradually like a migraine.

list.title: Severe pain:
list.snippet: It may be described as the worst headache of your life, or significantly more painful than your usual headaches.

list.title: Location:
list.snippet: The pain may be localized to a specific area, potentially linked to the location of the stroke in the brain. For example, a stroke in the carotid artery may cause pain in the forehead or face.

list.title: Other symptoms:
list.snippet: It can be accompanied by other stroke symptoms like:
Facial drooping: One side of the face may droop or feel numb.
Weakness or numbness: This can affect one side of the body, especially the arm or leg.
Speech difficulties: Slurred speech or trouble understanding others.
Vision problems: Blurred vision, double vision, or loss of vision.
Dizziness or loss of balance: Difficulty walking or coordinating movements.
Confusion or memory loss: Difficulty thinking clearly or remembering things.

list.title: Not all headaches are strokes:
list.snippet: Many headaches are not related to stroke. However, if you experience a severe headache with any of the other symptoms mentioned above, it's crucial to seek immediate medical attention.

list.title: Thunderclap headaches:
list.snippet: These are extremely severe headaches that come on suddenly and require immediate emergency care.

list.title: Migraines:
list.snippet: While some migraine symptoms can overlap with stroke symptoms, migraines typically have a gradual onset and are often accompanied by aura, nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound.
If you experience a sudden, severe headache with any of the associated stroke symptoms, call emergency services (911 in the US) immediately.
Early treatment is crucial for stroke recovery, so don't hesitate to seek medical attention if you suspect a stroke.

related_questions.question: Why am I getting headaches all of a sudden?

text_blocks.snippet: Sudden headaches can stem from various causes, including stress, dehydration, or even changes in the weather. Less common causes include underlying medical conditions like brain aneurysms or infections. If the headaches are severe or persistent, it's crucial to seek medical advice.
snippet_highlighted_words: stress, dehydration, or even changes in the weather

list.snippet: Stress: Both physical and emotional stress can trigger tension headaches, which are characterized by a dull, aching pain.
Dehydration: Not drinking enough fluids can lead to headaches as the brain becomes deprived of essential nutrients.
Weather Changes: Fluctuations in air pressure or temperature can trigger headaches in some individuals.
Lack of Sleep: Insufficient or disrupted sleep can contribute to tension headaches.
Caffeine Withdrawal: If you regularly consume caffeine, suddenly stopping can cause headaches.
Dietary Factors: Certain foods, like those with nitrates or excessive amounts of alcohol, can trigger headaches in some people.
Eyestrain: Prolonged periods of focusing on close-up tasks can lead to headaches.

text_blocks.snippet: Less Common, but Potentially Serious Causes:

list.snippet: Infections: Infections like sinusitis can cause headaches due to inflammation and pressure.
Brain Aneurysms or Blood Clots: These can cause severe headaches and require immediate medical attention.
Brain Tumors: While rare, brain tumors can also cause headaches.
Medication Overuse: Using pain relievers too frequently can lead to rebound headaches.
Head Injury: Any head trauma, even minor, can result in headaches.
High Blood Pressure: In some cases, severe hypertension can trigger headaches.
Headaches accompanied by fever, stiff neck, confusion, or vision changes.
Headaches that are sudden, severe, or unlike any you've experienced before.
Headaches that don't respond to over-the-counter pain relievers or home remedies.
Headaches that interfere with your daily activities or cause significant pain.
Headaches that persist for several days or weeks.
